title: Hit an incoming air hockey puck into the far goal with a held mallet
instruction: Play air hockey: hold the mallet by its handle and hit the puck that slides toward you so that it goes into the far goal. Keep the mallet on your half and your hands off the puck.
context: Hitting a moving puck needs timing and aim at once. The puck comes down the left of the table, so simply blocking it knocks it back into the end rail beside the goal: the mallet has to meet it moving, at an angle that sends it across to the goal.
setup: A tabletop air hockey game stands on the table, its long axis pointing away from the robot: a rigid blue playfield 600 mm long and 320 mm wide whose top is 60 mm above the table, its near end 220 mm in front of the line through the arm bases and its long axis straight ahead of the robot, midway between the arm bases. A halfway line is marked across it 300 mm from each end. Red plastic rails 20 mm high and 15 mm thick run round it, with a 90 mm goal slot centred in each end rail (a white box behind each slot catches the puck); the near goal is the robot's. The puck: a black plastic disc 50 mm across, 6 mm thick, 10 g, lying 80 mm from the far end and 80 mm left of the long axis (as the robot sees it). The mallet: a yellow plastic disc 60 mm across and 12 mm thick with a handle 24 mm across and 35 mm tall on top, 50 g, its centre on the long axis, 40 mm from the near end rail (in front of the robot's goal), 25 mm clear of the puck's path. A practice kicker is fixed at the far end: a grey plastic block 20 x 50 x 14 mm, 15 mm behind the puck. (For a real trial: a 50 mm sled on a straight rail, drawn back 40 mm against a compression spring to a latch whose pin a hobby servo pulls on a timer; the spring is checked before each set of trials so the puck takes 0.22 to 0.25 s between two marks 200 mm apart.) Seven seconds into the trial it pushes 40 mm toward the robot and sends the puck straight down the left of the table (80 mm left of the long axis) at about 0.85 m/s; it reaches the robot's end about 0.6 s later. Unhit, it stops against the near end rail beside the goal. Nothing else is on the table; the screenshot shows the start.
scoring: Read from an overhead slow-motion video at 240 fps (a phone's slow-motion mode) with the halfway line and the goals marked. A hit: the puck, coming toward the robot, turns back (moving away at 0.05 m/s or more) at the mallet, with all of: the mallet's rim within 30 mm of the puck's in the frames either side of the turn, the mallet held (a gripper's fingers closed on its handle), the mallet itself moving at 0.2 m/s or more over the 0.1 s before (a strike: a mallet held still in the puck's way is not a hit), and the puck's edge at least 10 mm from the near end rail (not a rebound off the rail). 1.0 if, after a hit, the puck goes into the far goal (crosses the far end within the 90 mm slot); 0.5 if, after a hit, it crosses the halfway line moving away from the robot but misses the goal; 0.25 for a hit that doesn't reach the halfway line; 0 with no hit. Any trial scores 0 if any part of the mallet crosses the halfway line (each player keeps to their half), if a gripper comes within 15 mm of the puck's edge, or if the puck goes into the robot's own goal. The simulation applies the same rules at 20 Hz; held there is a gripper's TCP within 20 mm of the mallet's axis at the handle's height with the fingers closed past half open.
run_limit: 600 steps (30 s at 20 Hz); the puck is sent 7 s in
reset_notes: Puck and mallet back to their marked spots, the launcher's sled drawn back to its latch and the servo timer reset; nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Isaac Sim rigid bodies. The air cushion is a nearly frictionless playfield (friction 0.02). The mallet's rim returns 75% of the puck's speed (est.); rails and goal boxes are dead, so bank shots are not modelled. Spin and air flow are not modelled. The kicker is a driven slider standing in for a spring launcher (see setup). Real trial: a battery tabletop game of about this size, e.g. a Relaxdays 10022514; record its model and sizes.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (600 steps, the run limit); demo: 1.0 (scripted, success at step 159)
